Contrasted with his [single season record ball](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popov_v._Hayashi) which resulted in years of litigation and controversy. 

One of the first cases in Property I of law school.

Well, MLB has a policy that when a ball leaves the field, it is considered abandoned by the league. Abandoned property goes to whoever first possesses it. This case was about whether or not Popov possessed the ball, and thus, had ownership. If he does have ownership, nobody can immediately profit. The court found that he did not but that he did have a “legally protected prepossessory interest” - which doesn’t really exist but they were trying to find a way to not screw him over - and had a right to half the profits. 

This case is compared with [Pierson v. Post](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierson_v._Post) where one hunter chases a fox but has not yet captured it and another hunter swoops in and captures it after it was tired out.
